lesson_title: Five Weeks From One Gunshot to a World War
hook_text: 28 June 1914. One gunshot in Sarajevo. Five weeks later, half the world is at war. How?
clip_script: 28 June 1914, Sarajevo. Gavrilo Princip shoots Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary. A month later, Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia. Russia protects Serbia. Germany backs Austria and declares war on Russia, then France. It marches through Belgium. Britain promised to protect Belgium, so Britain is in. Five weeks. One gunshot. Why so fast? Because the room was already full of gas. Militarism: everyone building armies and battleships. Alliances: promises to back each other up. Imperialism: racing to grab colonies. Nationalism: fierce national pride. MAIN. The shot was just the spark. And South Africa? As part of the British Empire, it was at war from day one. At Delville Wood in 1916, about 3 000 South Africans held a wood for six days; fewer than 800 answered the roll call. In 1917 the SS Mendi sank in the English Channel and more than 600 men of the Native Labour Corps died. Remember them.
visual_style: A pistol shot freezes on a 1914 street; a map of Europe lights up country by country with arrows; four letters M A I N appear as gas filling a room; a match drops; cut to a shattered wood and a ship sinking in fog.
pacing: Rapid-fire chain of declarations, a pause for MAIN, a slower, sombre close on South Africa.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for trench warfare, South Africa's role and how to judge a historical source.
